# Week 3, Day 4.1 — TypeScript for conditional skipping

Two small things. Today you switch tests off — sometimes always, sometimes only on one browser.

> **Every Run starts fresh.** The studio executes your code in a new process each time, so nothing is left over between runs.

| # | Concept | Why today needs it |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `===` and booleans | `test.skip(browserName === "firefox")` is just a comparison |
| 2 | Passing a condition as an argument | the skip decision is computed, then handed over |

Already covered — one link each: objects in [Day 1.1](/learn/w3/d1/p1); `let`/`const` and arrow
functions in [Day 2.1](/learn/w3/d2/p1).

## 1. `===` produces a boolean

`===` asks "are these exactly the same?" and answers `true` or `false`. Nothing more.

Use `===`, not `==`. The two-character version converts types before comparing, which produces
results nobody wants — `0 == ""` is `true`.

**Expected:** `true`, `false`, `isFirefox: true | type: boolean`, then `true` and `false`.

That last pair is the whole argument for `===`. In a skip condition, a surprising `true` means a
test silently stops running and nobody notices for months.

**Challenge:** set `browserName` to `"webkit"` and predict all four lines before re-running.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## 2. Handing a condition to a function

`test.skip()` takes the **answer**, not the question. You compute `true`/`false` first, and the
second argument is the reason — which ends up in the report.

```ts
test.skip(browserName === "firefox", "BUG-1508: Firefox mis-renders the tile grid");
```

**Expected:**

```
chromium   running
firefox    SKIPPED — BUG-1508
webkit     running
```

One test, three outcomes, decided by a comparison. That is all conditional skipping is.

**Always pass a reason.** A bare `test.skip(true)` in six months is a test nobody can justify
deleting or restoring.

## Recap

| Concept | Remember |
|---|---|
| `===` | Strict. Never use `==`. |
| Booleans | `test.skip()` takes the answer, plus a reason. |

# Week 3, Day 4.2 — Switching tests off, on purpose

A test fails because of a defect you've already logged. You don't want red every run, and you
don't want to delete the test. By the end of this lesson you'll know the four ways Playwright
offers, and which one to reach for.

> **Mode: test-runner.** This part is about running specs with the Playwright test runner. The studio editor runs library code, so follow these along in your own checkout.

## Why not just comment it out?

That's the habit from older tools, and it's the worst option:

| Commented-out body | `test.skip` |
|---|---|
| invisible in the report | appears as **skipped**, with a reason |
| stops compiling — rots quietly | still type-checked and reviewed |
| no record of why | the reason is in the code and the report |
| easy to forget forever | shows up every run as unfinished business |

A skipped test is a *visible* piece of debt. A commented-out one is just gone.

## The four tools

| Form | Runs? | Use it when |
|---|---|---|
| `test.skip(true, "reason")` | never | a known defect, everywhere |
| `test.skip(cond, "reason")` | when `cond` is false | the defect is browser- or env-specific |
| `test.fixme(...)` | never | same as skip; the older name |
| `test.only(...)` | **only this one** | debugging, locally, never committed |

`fixme` came first. The team added `skip` because it reads better, and kept `fixme` so existing
suites didn't break. Same effect — prefer `skip` in new code.

## Example 1 — skip and fixme, in a real spec

The cell below writes the spec and runs it under the **root config**, which enables Chromium only.

> ▶ **Run it yourself:** `npx playwright test week3/generated/day4-skipping.spec.ts`

**Expected:** `3 passed`, `2 skipped`.

Five tests, three ran. The two `skip`/`fixme` tests report as **skipped, not failed** — the suite
is green *and* honest about what isn't covered.

Both conditional tests ran here, because their conditions ask about Firefox and WebKit and this
config only has Chromium. `false` means "don't skip", so they behaved like normal tests.

## Example 2 — conditional skipping needs more than one browser

The root config enables Chromium only, and it's shared by every week — so instead of editing it,
Day 4 brings its own config with three browsers.

The cell below writes that config plus the spec, then runs the spec across all three.

> ▶ **Run it yourself:** `npx playwright test -c week3/generated/day4-browsers.config.ts`

**Expected:** `7 passed`, `8 skipped` — 15 in total.

Five tests times three browsers is 15. Where the 8 skips come from:

| Test | chromium | firefox | webkit |
|---|---|---|---|
| normal test | pass | pass | pass |
| unconditional skip | skip | skip | skip |
| `fixme` | skip | skip | skip |
| skip on Firefox | pass | **skip** | pass |
| skip on WebKit | pass | pass | **skip** |

That's 3 + 3 + 1 + 1 = 8 skipped, 7 passed.

**This is the payoff.** The Firefox defect costs you Firefox coverage of one test — not the test,
and not the browser. Deleting the test or removing Firefox from the config would have thrown away
far more.

## `test.only` — useful, and dangerous

You're debugging one test in a file of twenty. Rather than skip nineteen, mark the one:

```ts
test.only("the one I am working on", async ({ page }) => { … });
```

**Never commit it.** `only` filters the *whole run*, not just its file. Measured on this repo:

| | Tests run |
|---|---|
| normal | **40 passed** |
| with one stray `test.only` in one file | **1 passed** |

Thirty-nine tests silently stopped running, and the suite still reported green. That's why this
lesson's spec deliberately contains no `only`, and why the root config sets `forbidOnly` under CI
— it turns the mistake into a build failure instead of a quiet gap.

Try it by hand: add `.only` to one test, run the suite, watch the count collapse, then remove it.

## Best practices

- **Always give a reason**, ideally a ticket number.
- **Prefer conditional over blanket skips** — keep the coverage you can.
- **Never commit `test.only`.**
- **Review skips periodically.** A skip from a year ago is either a fixed bug or a dead test.
- **Prefer `skip` over `fixme`** in new code.

## Common mistakes

| You see | Usually means | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Suite passes but covers almost nothing | a committed `test.only` | remove it; rely on `forbidOnly` in CI |
| A skip that nobody can explain | no reason given | always pass one |
| `test.skip()` outside a test | it needs the condition inside the test body | put it as the first line |
| Conditional skip never fires | only one browser configured | check the config's `projects` |
| Skipped test still counted as failure | it isn't — that's a misread report | skipped and failed are separate columns |

**Next:** [Day 4.3](/learn/w3/d4/p3) — what skips look like on a real team.

# Week 3, Day 4.3 — Skips as a managed list

Same `test.skip` as [Day 4.2](/learn/w3/d4/p2). No new API. What changes is treating skips as debt
with an owner rather than a switch you flick.

## The failure mode

Skips are easy to add and nobody's job to remove. Three years on, a suite has forty of them, and
nobody knows which bugs are fixed. Coverage looks fine — the report is green — while a fifth of
the suite hasn't run since 2024.

| Skip that ages well | Skip that rots |
|---|---|
| `test.skip(true, "BUG-1421: stale balance")` | `test.skip(true)` |
| names a ticket someone can look up | names nothing |
| conditional — still covers other browsers | blanket |
| reviewed when the ticket closes | never revisited |

The difference is entirely in the second argument.

**Expected:** three lines, the last flagged as older than 90 days.

A team that writes reasons in a consistent shape can grep for them and build exactly this list.
A team that writes `test.skip(true)` cannot, at any price.

## Where the choice actually lives

| Situation | Reach for |
|---|---|
| Defect on one browser | `test.skip(browserName === "x", "TICKET")` |
| Feature not deployed to this environment | `test.skip(!!process.env.STAGING, "…")` |
| Test is slow, not broken | `test.slow()` — not a skip |
| Test is wrong, not the app | fix or delete it — a skip hides your bug |
| Whole area under rebuild | `test.describe.skip(...)` on the group |

That fourth row is the one people get wrong. A skip says *the application is broken*. If the
**test** is broken, skipping it files your mistake under someone else's name.

## What a reviewer checks

- **Every skip has a ticket**, not just prose.
- **Conditional where possible** — don't discard coverage you could keep.
- **No `test.only`** anywhere, ever.
- **`forbidOnly` enabled in CI** (this repo's root config does).
- **Skips have an age** — if nobody knows when it was added, that's the real problem.

**Next:** [Day 4.4](/learn/w3/d4/p4) — your turn.

# Week 3, Day 4.4 — Practice

Three problems. No answer key.

App: `https://test-automation-banking.vercel.app/`. Multi-browser config:
`week3/generated/day4-browsers.config.ts` (chromium, firefox, webkit — all verified installed).

> Stuck past twenty minutes? Back to [Day 4.1](/learn/w3/d4/p1) or [Day 4.2](/learn/w3/d4/p2).

## When you're done

**Count your skips and ask who owns each one.** A skip with a ticket has an owner and an end
date. A skip without one is a permanent hole in your coverage that the green tick is actively
hiding from you.

**Next:** [Day 5.1](/learn/w3/d5/p1) — running everything across three browsers, in parallel.

problems.statement:
**Build.** A spec with four tests where exactly two run.

1. One that passes normally
2. One skipped unconditionally, with a ticket number in the reason
3. One using `test.fixme`
4. One that passes normally

**Check yourself.** The tally reads `2 passed, 2 skipped`. Open the HTML report and confirm the
skipped ones show your reasons — if a reason is missing, you passed only one argument.

> **Hint** — `test.skip()` goes as the **first line inside** the test body, not outside it.

**Build.** Browser-specific skips, and predict the arithmetic before you run.

Write three tests against the dashboard. Skip one on Firefox only, one on WebKit only, and let
the third run everywhere.

**Before running**, write down your predicted passed/skipped counts across three browsers. Then
run it with the Day 4 config.

**Check yourself.** Your prediction matches. If not, work out why before changing anything — the
arithmetic is 3 tests × 3 browsers, minus one skip each for two of them.

> **Hint** — the answer is 7 and 2. Knowing *why* is the exercise.

**Build.** A skip that responds to the environment, not the browser.

Some tests should only run against a staging deployment. Write a spec where:

1. Two tests always run
2. One runs **only** when an environment variable `RUN_SLOW` is set
3. One is skipped on **both** Firefox and WebKit in a single condition
4. Every skip names a reason

Then run it three ways and record the tallies: default; with `RUN_SLOW=1`; and with the
multi-browser config.

**Where.** A spec in `week3/generated/`.

**Constraints — these are the exercise:**

- **No `test.only`**
- **No edit to the root `playwright.config.ts`**
- Every skip reason names a ticket or a condition a stranger could evaluate

**Check yourself.** Three runs, three different tallies, all green. Then answer in a comment:
*which of these four tests would you be most nervous about six months from now, and why?*

> **Hint** — for one condition covering two browsers, remember a boolean can be built from an
> array. And `process.env.RUN_SLOW` is a string or `undefined`, never a boolean.
